newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan land scheme seen breathing life into market.
newsitem.headline: Japan land scheme seen breathing life into market.

text.p: The Japanese government on Tuesday said it will announce plans to boost liquidity in the nation's land market by the end of the month, in a move analysts said would breathe life into the stagnant market.
But they added that brisk turnover in the real estate market was not going to happen overnight.

"It's a step forward and the stock market reacted quickly this morning, but turning bad land into good land is something you do bit by bit. It will take a very long time," said Hisanori Ito, an analyst at Nikko Research Center.

Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka told a news conference on Tuesday morning that measures to improve land liquidity, focusing on securitising collateralised land, would be drawn up by the government by March 31.
He said the land liquidity scheme would help bring land prices to levels where they should be and help financial firms burdened with problem loans.
"If we make effective use of land, then it is true that this will have an impact on solving problem loans quickly for financial firms," he told a news conference.
The announcement pushed stocks in the real estate and banking sectors higher and sent the dollar slightly lower against the yen on Tuesday morning.

Japanese banks are struggling with a mountain of bad loans, many of which were made to the real estate sector and used property as collateral. Official figures put the amount of bad loans at nearly 30 trillion yen ($243 billion) but some estimates have put the figure at twice that amount.
Most analysts said they expected the securitisation scheme would not work with tax reforms and would be centred around tax incentives.

"Acquisition tax, registration tax, capital gains tax - they all make buying and selling land in Japan very costly. It's got to be about making the property more attractive for the buyer," said Tokumatsu Iida, an analyst at Lehman Brothers.

Steven Weiler, an analyst at Jardine Fleming Securities, said the steps for securitising collateralised property are only likely to relate to loans of failed housing firms now administered by a special body and not the market as a whole.

He says the government could follow the precedents set by some domestic banks such as Sanwa Bank Ltd and Fuji Bank Ltd which have set up special purpose companies to administer such loans - but the problem of who would guarantee the loans remained an obstacle.
"The government could guarantee the loans but that would require some tweaking of the format," he said.
Nikko Research's Ito said it would be difficult for the government to guarantee the securities as it would be like guaranteeing that a certain company's stocks would not fall below a certain level.
Some analysts doubted that a workable securitisation system could be easily planned.

"Investors will be looking for small lot products with good interest rates and where the capital is guaranteed. However it would be difficult to come up with such products while land prices are still falling," said one analyst.
He added that for collateralised land there would remain problems of who would bear the responsibility for securitising the land when there was more than one owner.

The land liquidity scheme follows draft proposals to relax construction regulations for condominium building, and analysts also expect it to include plans to use public funds to buy collateralised land for parks and old-age homes.

But they also said buying of land for parks while helping developers and financial firms holding such land, had little to do with creating new business and would not lead to more liquidity in the market. ($1=123 yen)
